1 big thing: GTA VI hijacks America
 
An ad for "Grand Theft Auto VI" in Times Square last week. Photo: Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images

The internet's warring tribes converged yesterday for the loud, lawless debut of "Grand Theft Auto VI," as 13 years of anticipation culminated in one of the great viral spectacles of all time, Axios' Herb Scribner and Zachary Basu write.

💰 By last night, GTA VI had generated an estimated $2.36 billion in sales from nearly 25 million copies — almost triple the first-day revenue of its record-breaking predecessor in 2013, according to Sensor Tower.

  • Millions of players have already downloaded the game to their consoles, with many taking time off work. GTA is "the Star Wars of this generation," Joost van Dreunen, adjunct professor at NYU Stern School of Business, told Reuters.
  • Gameplay clips have already amassed tens of billions of views across X, TikTok, YouTube and other platforms.

🐊 Zoom in: GTA VI drops players into Vice City, a fictionalized Miami that serves as a sprawling digital fever dream of violence, celebrity, corruption and distinctly American absurdity.

  • Players can rob banks, steal planes, wrestle alligators and wreak havoc — or pass the afternoon by fishing, shopping, working out and tending to the relationships among the game's characters.
A scene from Vice City in "Grand Theft Auto VI." Image: Rockstar Games

Zoom out: GTA's return has revived decades-old arguments about whether violent video games encourage real-world aggression, while igniting a far stranger debate over masculinity.

  • The White House posted a minute-long Trump montage, "WELCOME TO MAGA CITY XLVII 🇺🇸🌴," using GTA's font to proclaim "47: The Golden Age."

🎮 "GTA Flu" was coined in 2013 when untold thousands of gamers took days off work to dive headfirst into San Andreas, the game's fictionalized version of Southern California.

  • A GameSquare survey found that 30% of employed U.S. gamers were considering taking time off to play.
  • At Fort Stewart, Georgia, 43 soldiers committed to another two to six years of Army service after a four-day GTA gaming pass was included as a reenlistment incentive.

The bottom line: GTA offers a glimpse of what monoculture looks like in 2026. For one extraordinary day, the internet had a common story — and a thousand different ways of telling it.

2. 🏗️ Senate passes build-faster bill
 

Illustration: Shoshana Gordon/Axios
 

The Senate passed a sweeping, bipartisan bill last night designed to cut permitting timelines for energy and infrastructure projects, Axios' Ben Geman reports.

  • The 62-33 vote is the first major action by Congress since midterms.

Why it matters: The eyes of the entire energy industry are on this bill. If it becomes law, it could transform how America builds energy infrastructure, with major implications for everything from electricity costs to data centers.

  • Getting rid of bureaucratic hurdles and creating a more predictable process for energy projects is a top priority for the fossil fuels and renewables sectors.

☀️ Between the lines: The bill also highlights a dilemma for environmentalists — building the infrastructure needed to fight climate change can threaten the very nature they're trying to protect, Axios' Amy Harder writes.

  • Wind and solar farms, for example, can require large expanses of land, potentially disrupting wildlife habitats even while helping reduce emissions.
  • Supporters of the bill say the current system takes too long, delaying clean energy and other infrastructure. Opponents warn speeding things up could come at the expense of wildlife, public lands and tribal rights.

What's next: The bill heads to the House. Speaker Mike Johnson told Bloomberg last week that he expects it to pass.

3. 🗳️ Religious "nones" take office
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

America's religious "nones" have gained a foothold in Congress: Five lawmakers will claim no religious affiliation in January, up from a single member just two years ago, Axios' Russell Contreras reports.

  • Why it matters: Washington remains far more religious than the nation it represents. But the last two election cycles have begun to change that.

🧮 By the numbers: Religiously unaffiliated voters made up 27% of the 2026 midterm electorate, up from 23% in 2024, according to preliminary Fox News voter polling.

  • Three lawmakers who claimed no religious affiliation — Reps. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.), Abraham Hamadeh (R-Ariz.) and Emily Randall (D-Wash.) — won reelection in November. They'll be joined in January by Democratic Reps.-elect Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania and Fred Wellman of Missouri — who publicly acknowledged their nonreligious identities before winning their Nov. 3 elections.

Zoom out: The nonreligious political bench stretches well beyond Capitol Hill.

  • More than 100 openly nonreligious lawmakers are expected to serve in at least 38 state legislatures, up from 81 in 33 states, according to the Center for Freethought Equality.

4. 🪖 Trump to skeptical Europeans: "Putin wants to end the war"
 

Photo illustration: Maura Kearns/Axios. Photos: Win McNamee/Getty Images, Getty Images Europe via Getty Images.
 

On his way back from China yesterday aboard Air Force One, President Trump phoned in to a meeting his envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were holding in Berlin with a group of European leaders and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, Axios' Barak Ravid reports.

  • Trump said, according to people in the room: "Putin wants to end the war, he wants the deal done, he is getting tired of this."

Why it matters: Instead of turning his historic trilateral summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin into a modern-day Yalta Conference, as some European and Ukrainian officials feared, Trump tried to use it to propel his push for peace in Europe.

  • Yes, but: At least one U.S. peace deal reportedly on the table would require Ukraine to surrender territory it still controls in the Donbas region in exchange for NATO membership.

👀 Behind the scenes: When Trump called in to brief the European leaders, he urged them to engage directly with Putin.

  • Trump said, referring to the German host: "Friedrich, you can make a call to Putin and this will make a deal ... Xi respects Zelensky. Putin is ready to do the deal. Zelensky can do a great deal."

5. 🤖 Anthropop!
 
Data: Financial Modeling Prep. Chart: Erin Davis/Axios

Anthropic delivered on the hype: The stock opened at $111.50 — a 34% lift from its $83 offering price — before closing at $97.17.

  • The company closed at a market cap of about $1.25 trillion, making it one of the most valuable businesses in the world, Axios' Emily Peck writes.
Left: Today's New York Post, California edition. Right: Dario Amodei speaks yesterday at the Nasdaq MarketSite in Manhattan. Photo: Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images

👀 The big picture: There was hope that a big Day 1 pop (an Anthropop, perhaps) would lift the AI trade. It did not.

  • The tech-heavy Nasdaq finished the day down 2.25% and is down 9.6% for the past 30 days.

Stunning stat: After the first day of trading, Anthropic's 5,300 founders and employees are worth more than the bottom third of U.S. households — 45 million families, according to financial analyst Steve Rattner's calculations.

6. 🗳️ Ossoff wins open-ended '28 poll
 
Graphic: Emerson College Polling (Poll of 1,000 U.S. voters, Nov. 14-16. Margin of error for full poll: ± 3 points.)

When Emerson College Polling asked Democratic voters to name their 2028 presidential choice without giving them a list, newly reelected Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia drew 17%, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez got 12%, California Gov. Gavin Newsom got 8% and Kamala Harris got 6%.

  • Why it matters: Harris often leads 2028 Democratic polls when the choices are set, reflecting her universal name ID.

🐘 In an open-ended question on the Republican side, 36% of GOP voters named Marco Rubio, 20% JD Vance, 7% Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, 7% President Trump and 7% maverick Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky.

  • Between the lines: Rubio has made no move to run. So the result captures the post-midterm angst for Vance.

Data: U.S. Department of Transportation, Bureau of Transportation Statistics. Table: Brad Jennings/Axios

Nearly a quarter of U.S. flights arrived at least 15 minutes late in November and December 2025, according to Axios' Brad Jennings' analysis of federal airline data.

8. 🥧 1 for the road: $35 Thanksgiving
 

Photo illustration: Lindsey Bailey/Axios. Photo: Library of Congress
 

The average cost of a Thanksgiving feast for 10 will be $58.63 this season, up 6% from last year.

  • The increase is driven by price hikes for turkey, milk, rolls and cranberries, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation.

Zoom in: Walmart is advertising a cheaper Thanksgiving meal than in 2025, Axios' Julianna Bragg reports.

  • The retailer said this year's bundle, which serves 10 people for $35, is its lowest-priced one-click basket ever, down from $39.93 last year.

The complete meal comes with a turkey, multiple sides and pumpkin pie to finish.

  • It adds ingredients for sweet potato casserole and corn muffins, but drops macaroni and cheese and baby carrots from last year's spread.
